panels.description: The percentage of CPU used by the database server process. 0-100.
panels.title: CPU Usage

panels.description: Procedure invocations completed per second on each node. In a K-safe cluster each transaction executes on every copy of its partition, and multi-partition work runs on all partitions, so this counts that fan-out and can exceed the rate of requests your application actually sends.
panels.title: TPS per node
Request latency percentiles (per node, whole transaction path)

panels.description: Median initiator latency per node: the time from a request arriving on the network to the response being sent back, including queueing, execution and, in a K-safe cluster, the wait for all partition copies to confirm.
panels.title: P50 latency

panels.description: 95th-percentile initiator latency per node - the full request-to-response time, including queueing, execution, and the K-safety replication wait. A good headline for what your slower requests experience.
panels.title: P95 latency

panels.description: 99th-percentile initiator latency per node - the full request-to-response time, including queueing, execution, and the K-safety replication wait. Use it to track tail latency.
panels.title: P99 latency

panels.description: 99.9th-percentile and observed maximum initiator latency per node - the full request-to-response time, including queueing, execution, and the K-safety replication wait. Surfaces the rare worst-case stalls.
panels.title: P99.9 / Max latency

panels.description: How long requests wait in the inbound queue before the cluster starts executing them, shown as median and 99th percentile per node. This is the first leg of initiator latency; rising values mean work is arriving faster than it can start executing, before any procedure even runs.
panels.title: Inbound queue wait (p50 / p99)

panels.description: The time to receive acknowledgment from partition replicas, shown as median and 99th percentile per node - the extra wait K-safety adds to every transaction. Empty when K = 0. If tail latency rises while procedure execution stays flat, look here: a slow or overloaded node makes every transaction on that partition wait for its replica.
panels.title: Replication round-trip (p50 / p99)

panels.description: How often transactions arrive at a node that is not the right one for their partition and must be forwarded on, per second per node - i.e. misrouted requests. Each misroute adds an extra network hop of latency; a sustained rate usually means clients are not topology-aware and can be fixed on the client side.
panels.title: Misrouted transactions rate
Procedure execution time — Procedure level (per node)

panels.description: Average procedure execution time per node - the procedure body only, excluding queueing, network, and the wait for partition replicas. Compare with the round-trip panels below to see how much the transaction path adds on top of the procedure itself.
panels.title: Avg execution time ($procedure)

panels.description: Peak procedure execution time per node - the procedure body only, excluding queueing, network, and the wait for partition replicas.
panels.title: Max execution time ($procedure)
Procedure execution time — Initiator level (per node)

panels.description: Average initiator latency per node per procedure: the whole transaction from request received to response sent, including queueing, execution and, in a K-safe cluster, the wait for every partition copy to confirm.
panels.title: Avg round-trip ($procedure)

panels.description: Peak initiator latency per node per procedure - the whole request-to-response transaction time, including queueing, execution, and the K-safety replication wait.
panels.title: Max round-trip ($procedure)
Command queue depth by site
panels.description: Number of tasks waiting to run at each execution site. A queue that stays deep or keeps growing means that site is falling behind its incoming work - a hot partition or an overloaded node - and shows up as rising latency.

How long tasks wait in the queue before they start executing, shown as median, 90th, and 99th percentiles. Rising wait times mean queued work is adding delay before execution and are an early warning of overload on a partition or node.
panels.title: Command queue wait time percentiles by site

panels.description: How often memory compaction runs on each node. Compaction reclaims unused memory from tables and indexes; frequent runs consume CPU and can coincide with brief latency increases.
panels.title: Compaction invocations (rate)

panels.description: Overlay compaction rate and in-progress snapshots to correlate with latency spikes.
panels.title: Compaction & snapshot activity

panels.description: How long it takes to create a new command-log file on disk (99th percentile). Rising times point to a slow or busy disk holding the command log.
panels.title: Command log segment allocation time (p99)

panels.description: How often the command log applies backpressure on each node. Backpressure happens when transactions are being committed faster than they can be written to disk, which throttles new work; sustained events mean disk write speed is limiting throughput.
panels.title: Command log backpressure (rate)
